text: We know. <break time="0.8s" /> That animals have evolved. <break time="0.8s" /> A variety of patterns to manipulate the perceptions of their predators. <break time="0.8s" /> To afford themselves a modicum of safety. <break time="0.8s" /> Greater Bower birds utilize perceptual biases. <break time="0.8s" /> In the mating domain. <break time="0.8s" /> Males construct a bower. <break time="0.8s" /> Its function is to provide an arena. <break time="0.8s" /> In which males display to females. <break time="0.8s" /> Standing in an avenue that leads up to the bower. <break time="0.8s" /> The males decorate the avenue. <break time="0.8s" /> With a variety of objects, such as stones and shells. <break time="0.8s" /> But they do not do so. <break time="0.8s" /> In a chaotic manner. <break time="0.8s" /> The larger objects are placed closer to the bower. <break time="0.8s" /> And the smaller objects farther away. <break time="0.8s" /> This creates a forced perspective the opposite of the Cinderella Castle. <break time="0.8s" /> The bower appears smaller. <break time="0.8s" /> Than it actually is. <break time="0.8s" /> Endler and his colleagues suggested. <break time="0.8s" /> That the male courting in the bower. <break time="0.8s" /> Now appears larger. <break time="0.8s" /> And thus more attractive to the female. <break time="0.8s" /> Data on male mating success collected in the wild. <break time="0.8s" /> Supports their hypothesis.
